# R7 Digest — Osborne, *Revelation* (BECNT 2002): IV Final Judgment (17:1–20:15)

**Source:** Grant R. Osborne, *Revelation*, Baker Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament (Baker Academic, 2002).  
**Range:** cache slice `R7_final_judgment_5693-6769.txt` (wiki lines 5693–6769) — Babylon the Great (17:1–19:5), parousia/rider (19:6–21), millennium (20:1–10), great white throne (20:11–15).  
**Extractor rules:** faithfulness only; no wiki edits; no material outside this slice; surveys attributed; no adjudication beyond Osborne.

---

## Claims

**C1.** Osborne frames 17:1–20:15 as the concluding judgment block of the scroll’s contents before the new creation: (1) 17:1–19:5 recapitulates seals/trumpets/bowls with new symbols (great prostitute, scarlet beast, Babylon; funeral laments); (2) 19:6–21 the parousia and destruction of evil powers; (3) ch. 20 millennium, final defeat of the dragon, and great white throne. Eternal punishment in the lake of fire unites 19–20 in three stages (beast/false prophet → devil → evildoers with Death and Hades).  
- *Locus:* intro to IV (slice ll. 3–7).  
- *Quote:* “This section features the lake of fire, with the evil forces being cast into eternal punishment in three stages, first the beast and the false prophet (19:20), then the devil (20:10), and finally the evildoers are thrown in along with Death and Hades (20:14–15).”

**C2.** The “hallelujah” material of 19:1–8 is a single holistic liturgy—the only NT use of “hallelujah”—yet Osborne divides it structurally: 19:1–5 concludes Babylon’s judgment; 19:6–8 introduces the parousia section, showing “the artificiality of all attempts to impose Western-style outlining on Near Eastern texts.”  
- *Locus:* intro to IV (slice l. 8).  
- *Quote:* “the ‘hallelujah’ section of 19:1–8 shows the artificiality of all attempts to impose Western-style outlining on Near Eastern texts.”

**C3.** Chapters 17–18 treat Rome/Babylon under two metaphors: ch. 17 as “great prostitute” drunk with saints’ blood (angelic interpretation of symbols); ch. 18 as “great city” destroyed (kings’, merchants’, sea captains’ laments). In 17:15–17 the beast and kings destroy the prostitute; in 18:10, 17, 19 God destroys the city “in one hour.”  
- *Locus:* 17:1–19:5 intro (slice ll. 27–28).  
- *Quote:* “Chapter 17 centers on Rome as the ‘great prostitute’… while chapter 18 then looks at Rome as ‘the great city’ destroyed.”

**C4.** The great prostitute is “Babylon the Great,” a symbol for Rome and the empire of the beast; πορνεία imagery depicts leading the world into immorality and religious apostasy/idolatry, with OT harlot cities (Nineveh, Tyre; apostate Israel/Jerusalem) as background.  
- *Locus:* 17:1–2 (slice ll. 76–77).  
- *Quote:* “She is ‘great’ because she is ‘Babylon the Great’… a symbol for Rome and the empire of the beast.”

**C5.** Survey of suggested “prostitute” antecedents (Jezebel of 2:20; Cleopatra; Messalina; goddess Roma): Osborne judges the image so general that only Dea Roma (coin of A.D. 71, seated on seven hills) is a plausible partial background; “Either way, the prostitute is clearly Babylon/Rome.”  
- *Locus:* 17:1–2 (slice l. 78).  
- *Quote:* “the only likely antecedent might be the goddess Roma… Either way, the prostitute is clearly Babylon/Rome, depicted in all her alluring depravity.”

**C6.** Against feminist/deconstructive readings that treat the whore as misogynistic “sexual murder” of colonized women (Pippin; J. Kim), Osborne cites Callahan: forensic, not salacious; “military language of urban siege.” In the additional note he agrees the whore is an OT/Greco-Roman symbol for immorality and apostasy, not a misogynistic rejection of women.  
- *Locus:* 17:1–2; Additional Note 17:1 (slice ll. 78, 221–22).  
- *Quote:* “When we read of the ‘whore of Babylon,’ we should read an ancient symbol for immorality and religious apostasy.”

**C7.** “Sits on many waters” (17:1; Jer. 51:13) = peoples, multitudes, nations, tongues (17:15)—control of the empire’s inhabitants; “kings of the earth” commit adultery with her, and earth-dwellers are drunk with the wine of her porneia (political-economic seduction by luxury/power is implicit here, clearer in ch. 18).  
- *Locus:* 17:1–2, 15 (slice ll. 80–82, 190).  
- *Quote:* “The ‘many waters’ are defined in 17:15 as ‘peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues,’ referring to the many nations under the control of Babylon/Rome.”

**C8.** Woman on scarlet beast (17:3–6): beast = political ruler (from 13:1: blasphemous names, seven heads, ten horns); woman = blasphemous religion that seduces nations **and** the economic system of earthly luxury; scarlet points to luxury. Four foci of Babylon: idolatry, immorality, luxury, persecution (“drunk with the blood of the saints… who witness to Jesus”).  
- *Locus:* 17:3–6a (slice ll. 88–100).  
- *Quote:* “While the beast is the political ruler of the empire, the woman represents the blasphemous religion that seduces the nations and the economic system that draws them into its earthly luxury.”

**C9.** “Mystery” on the forehead is not part of the name but marks end-time revelation (cf. 1:20; 10:7); Beale’s “ironic” self-destruction of evil (17:16) is noted. “Babylon the Great” echoes Dan. 4:30 and Jewish/Christian use of Babylon for Rome (1 Pet. 5:13; 2 Bar.; Sib. Or.; 4 Ezra). “Mother of prostitutes and abominations” = she reproduces immorality/idolatry in the nations.  
- *Locus:* 17:5 (slice ll. 94–96).  
- *Quote:* “In keeping with the use of ‘mystery’ in 1:20 and 10:7, the latter is more likely… The ‘mystery’ then is ‘Babylon the Great,’ telling us specifically that she represents the empire of the beast.”

**C10.** Beast “was and is not and is about to ascend from the abyss and go to destruction” (17:8) parodies God’s “was/is/is to come” and Christ’s death-resurrection; builds on Nero redivivus / mortal wound healed (13:3, 12, 14). Ascension “about to” = final Antichrist at history’s end (not merely repeated despots through history—contra Hendriksen/Mounce on that point as Osborne reads them). Destiny: prophetic present “going to destruction.”  
- *Locus:* 17:8 (slice ll. 112–14).  
- *Quote:* “all the imagery here points to the final appearance of the Antichrist at the end of history… His ‘destruction’ will be eternal (20:10).”

**C11.** Seven heads = seven mountains (= Rome’s seven hills) **and** seven kings (17:9–11). Osborne surveys seven historical/emperor-list solutions (Nero-era; Vespasian-vision/Domitian-writing; Caligula-start; Nero-start with pretenders; violent deaths/Nerva; empires not kings) and prefers a **combined symbolic-historical** view with Bauckham: 5+1+1 refers to Roman emperors with Domitian presupposed as reigning, but numbering is symbolic of temporary tyranny about to be completed, not a precise emperor cipher.  
- *Locus:* 17:9–11 (slice ll. 122–67).  
- *Quote:* “the 5 + 1 + 1 does refer to Roman emperors, and both John and his readers presupposed that the reigning emperor was Domitian… The numbering was not a reference to specific emperors, however, but a symbolic reference to the belief that the Roman tyranny was a temporary phenomenon about to be completed.”

**C12.** The beast as “eighth… of the seven” (17:11): not that he is literally Nero redivivus, but “like Nero in his character and destiny” (Michaels, endorsed). Eighth as parody of resurrection / “eighth day” is possible; gematria parody of Ἰησοῦς=888 vs 666 is noted; Osborne prefers resurrection-symbol meaning tied to “was/is not/is to come.”  
- *Locus:* 17:11 (slice ll. 168–70).  
- *Quote:* “The point is not that the eighth king is actually Nero redivivus, but that he is like Nero in his character and destiny.”

**C13.** Ten horns = ten kings yet to receive kingdoms (17:12–14): better as Roman-style **client kings** than provincial governors (with Aune); connected to “kings from the east” / Armageddon sequence (7:1; 16:12–16). Authority “for one hour” with the beast (great tribulation / three-and-a-half years). They give power/authority to the beast, then war against the Lamb, who conquers as “Lord of lords and King of kings”; “called, elect, and faithful” accompany him (saints participate—active holy-war type alongside more passive 19:14 imagery).  
- *Locus:* 17:12–14 (slice ll. 172–87).  
- *Quote:* “it is best to see the background in the Roman practice of appointing client kings… They will go to war along with the beast, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings.”

**C14.** Civil war: beast + ten horns hate, desolate, strip, devour, burn the prostitute (17:16; Ezek. 23:25–29 + Jezebel flesh motif); Caird: “self-destroying power of evil.” God “put it into their hearts” (17:17)—divine sovereignty over evil; purpose: fulfill “the words of God.” Woman = “the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth” (17:18).  
- *Locus:* 17:15–18 (slice ll. 190–207).  
- *Quote:* “For God has put it into their hearts to accomplish his purpose… until God’s words are fulfilled.”

**C15.** Against strict preterism (Rome lasted centuries; Jerusalem-as-woman stretches imagery), Osborne combines preterist, idealist, and futurist: primarily final Antichrist-Babylon, with Rome as image-base, embracing all Rome-like centers of power. Mounce: “Every great center of power that has prostituted its wealth and influences restores to life the spirit of ancient Babylon.”  
- *Locus:* 17:18 summary (slice ll. 207–08).  
- *Quote:* “This is primarily a prophecy of the final evil Babylon established by the Antichrist, but it still considers Rome the basis for the imagery and also embraces all the Rome-like cities of history.”

**C16.** Chapter 18’s overarching theme is judgment for **economic oppression**; Callahan: “critique in apocalyptic idiom of the political economy of ancient Rome.” Structure: angel’s fall announcement (1–3); heavenly voice—flee + lex talionis (4–8); three funeral laments (9–19); saints rejoice (20); millstone acted parable + desolation (21–24).  
- *Locus:* 18 intro (slice ll. 231–33).  
- *Quote:* “The overarching theme of this section is the judgment on Babylon/Rome for its economic oppression.”

**C17.** Angel announces “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the Great” (18:1–3; Isa. 21:9; cf. 14:8); desolation as home for demons/unclean spirits/birds (Isa. 13; Jer. 50–51, etc.). Nations fallen **because of** wine of her immorality (Osborne prefers πεπτωκαν “fallen” over “drunk/drunk” reading—additional note). Kings’ adultery (religious); merchants grown rich “because of the power of her luxuries”—materialistic luxury as major ch. 18 theme (Ezek. 27/Tyre).  
- *Locus:* 18:1–3; n. on 18:3 (slice ll. 382–400, 540).  
- *Quote:* “chapter 18 focuses on the economic sins of Rome and the luxurious ostentation that brings about the wrath of God.”

**C18.** “Come out from her, my people” (18:4): physical flight in narrative, spiritual separation for Asian churches—ethical faithfulness/perseverance. Sins “reached to heaven”; God “remembered her crimes” (judicial). Lex talionis 18:6–8: pay back as she paid; “double” debated—full requital (Kline et al.) vs. double penalty for severity/economic theft (Exod. 22); cup of wrath for cup of sin. Boast “I sit as a queen” (Isa. 47:7–9); plagues “in one day” = suddenly; “mighty is the Lord God who has judged her.”  
- *Locus:* 18:4–8 (slice ll. 404–40).  
- *Quote:* “This section is dominated by the lex talionis (law of retribution) theme… ‘pay her back as she has paid back [to others].’”

**C19.** Three laments (kings 9–10; merchants 11–17a; sea personnel 17b–19): form-critical parallels (stand far off; weep; “woe, woe”; “one hour”); built on Ezek. 27. Mourners grieve lost luxury, not sin—self-centered to the end. Cargo list (18:12–13) shows ostentatious Roman elite goods; slaves as “bodies… human souls” (negative livestock sense for Osborne).  
- *Locus:* 18:9–19 (slice ll. 442–98).  
- *Quote:* “None of these groups mourns their sin, only all the luxurious living they have lost.”

**C20.** Heaven/saints/apostles/prophets rejoice (18:20) because “God has judged her for the way she judged you”—lex talionis and vindication, not sadistic revenge. Beale: rejoicing defends God’s just name and shows the world’s verdict against the saints wrong. Millstone into sea (18:21; Jer. 51:63–64): future violent casting down; five “never again” losses (music, craftsmen, millstone, lamp, bridegroom/bride). Final charges: merchant arrogance (“economic self-idolatry”), deception by “sorcery” (metaphorical demonic deception), blood of prophets/saints and “all killed on the earth.”  
- *Locus:* 18:20–24 (slice ll. 500–26).  
- *Quote:* “It is justice that is being celebrated, not just the punishment itself.”

**C21.** Hallelujah choruses 19:1–5: only NT Ἁλληλουϊά; movement from multitude → elders/creatures → voice from throne. Multitude (likely triumphant saints, with 7:9) praises salvation/glory/power; “judgments are true and just”; judges the prostitute who corrupted the earth; avenges slaves’ blood (6:10 answered). Smoke of torment forever (19:3; cf. 14:11)—eternal punishment contrast to eternal God/saints. Voice from throne: divine authorization (not clearly God or Christ saying “our God”); calls slaves who fear him, small and great.  
- *Locus:* 19:1–5 (slice ll. 549–37).  
- *Quote:* “Only here in the NT does the word Ἁλληλουϊά… occur, and it governs 19:1–8.”

**C22.** Parousia section 19:6–21: for saints, wedding of the Lamb; for sinners, destruction in three stages (Christ arrives; birds invited to “great banquet of God”; battle/aftermath). “Great war… never really occurs”—armies gather, sword from mouth, instantly over. Beast/false prophet first into lake of fire.  
- *Locus:* 19:6–21 intro (slice ll. 661–67).  
- *Quote:* “Most of all, the great war for which the book has prepared since 16:14, 16 never really occurs… immediately the armies are no more.”

**C23.** Wedding of the Lamb (19:6–8): Lord God Almighty “has begun to reign” (ingressive aorist, as 11:17). Bride imagery from OT (Isa. 54; 61:10; Ezek. 16; Hos. 2) and NT (Matt. 22; 25; John 3:29; 2 Cor. 11:2; Eph. 5). Wife “prepared herself” by faithfulness/testimony/endurance/obedience; God “gave” fine linen (divine sovereignty + human preparation—Phil. 2:12–13). Fine linen = “righteous deeds of the saints” (subjective and objective genitive with Beale—deeds of saints and God’s vindicating acts). Contrast with prostitute’s purple/scarlet luxury.  
- *Locus:* 19:6–8 (slice ll. 728–47).  
- *Quote:* “The fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints… Here we have the two sides of the Christian life described in Phil. 2:12–13.”

**C24.** Beatitude: “Blessed are those invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb” (19:9)—saints as both bride and guests (mixed metaphors; not tribulation-bride vs. earlier guests). Messianic banquet tradition (Isa. 25:6; 1 Enoch 62; 2 Bar. 29; 4 Ezra 2; etc.). “True words of God” anchors 19:6–10 sayings. John falls to worship angel (19:10): common apocalyptic rejection-of-angel-worship motif; angels are fellow slaves; “testimony about Jesus is Spirit-inspired prophecy.”  
- *Locus:* 19:9–10 (slice ll. 749–62).  
- *Quote:* “Angels are not above human beings but equal to them… ‘testimony about Jesus is Spirit-inspired prophecy.’”

**C25.** Rider on white horse christology (19:11–16): heaven opened; white warhorse (not purity-garment white). Titles/qualities: “Faithful and True”; judges and makes war “in righteousness”; eyes like raging fire; many diadems (vs. dragon/beast’s diadems—true King of kings); name only he knows (eschatological essence; saints later share per 2:17); garment dipped in blood = **enemies’ blood** (Isa. 63; military context; chronology jumbled for rhetorical effect—not primarily atonement or martyrs’ blood); “Word of God”; armies of heaven (angels **and** saints) on white horses; sharp sword from mouth (Isa. 11:4; 49:2—proclamation **and** execution); shepherds with iron rod (Ps. 2:9—destroys predatory foes); treads winepress of God Almighty’s wrath (14:19–20; Isa. 63); name on garment/thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (divine title applied to Christ; cf. 17:14). Roman triumph imagery (Aune) noted.  
- *Locus:* 19:11–16 (slice ll. 766–806).  
- *Quote:* “Thus, Christ’s robe is dipped in the blood of his enemies, a reference to Isa. 63:1–3… He is also ‘the Word of God’… ‘King of kings and Lord of lords.’”

**C26.** Carrion-bird banquet (19:17–18; Ezek. 39:17–20) parodies wedding supper: two messianic banquets—saints feast **with** the Lamb; birds feast **on** sinners. List of victims is rhetorical for all who fight at Armageddon, **not** all earth-dwellers (some nations remain for 20:7–8). Battle (19:19–21): beast/kings/armies gathered (from 16:14–16); no prolonged fight; beast and false prophet seized, thrown **alive** into lake of fire (conscious punishment—problem for annihilationism); rest killed by sword from mouth; birds gorge (lex talionis for denying burial to two witnesses, 11:9).  
- *Locus:* 19:17–21 (slice ll. 808–33).  
- *Quote:* “There will be two great messianic banquets at the eschaton: the feast with the Lamb for the saints and the feast on the sinners for the carrion birds.”

**C27.** Lake of fire (19:20 first of four castings): Gehenna background (Hinnom; Jesus’ teaching) + apocalyptic fiery abyss/river (Dan. 7; 1 Enoch; etc.); “fire” from Sodom traditions, “lake” possibly Hellenistic hell portrayals (Bertrand).  
- *Locus:* 19:20 (slice ll. 826–29).  
- *Quote:* “Τὴν λίμνην τοῦ πυρός… occurs only in Rev. 19–21 in the NT… The basic connection with ‘Gehenna,’ of course, is certain.”

**C28.** **Millennial views survey (Osborne):** (1) **Premillennialism**—Christ returns, destroys evil, reigns on earth a thousand years; then Satan’s rebellion, final judgment, future age. (2) **Amillennialism**—no literal post-parousia earthly reign; 20:1–10 symbolic of church age between advents (Christ reigns now). (3) **Postmillennialism**—thousand years of gospel triumph/peace **precede** the second coming. Early chiliasm debates; Augustine’s amillennialism dominated ~1200 years; modern reopening via pietism, Puritan postmil, dispensational premil.  
- *Locus:* 20:1–10 intro (slice ll. 876–80).  
- *Quote:* “Since then three positions have often sorely divided Christian groups… premillennialism… Amillennialism… Postmillennialism…”

**C29.** **Osborne’s historic premillennial position and irenic stance:** “In this commentary, I take a premillennial approach but recognize the viability of the other two positions. This issue will not be solved until the events take place… Until then, we should not fight over these issues but be ‘iron sharpening iron’…” Premil preferred because it better fits narrative flow (parousia → millennium → final judgment → new creation) and “deceive the nations” / “came to life” language. Data “point more to a premillennial stance” though only one direct biblical passage teaches the millennium—hence no rigid fight.  
- *Locus:* 20 intro; summary (slice ll. 880, 978–80).  
- *Quote:* “I take a premillennial approach but recognize the viability of the other two positions… we should not fight over these issues but be ‘iron sharpening iron’ as we work together for the kingdom.”

**C30.** Function of 20:1–10 within the book (beyond millennial debate): judgment of the dragon in two stages (bound in abyss → lake of fire); **theodicy climax**—earth-dwellers experience Christ’s reign without satanic deception yet flock to Satan when released, justifying eternal punishment; vindication of saints who reign as priests/kings (2:26–27; 3:21; 1:6; 5:10). Rossing: counters Rome’s realized “golden age” millennial triumphalism with “not yet.”  
- *Locus:* 20 intro (slice ll. 884–87).  
- *Quote:* “One of the purposes of this passage is to justify the necessity of eternal punishment… even the equivalent of fourteen lifetimes… are not enough to overturn their allegiance to Satan.”

**C31.** Binding of Satan (20:1–3): angel with key of the abyss and great chain (possibly same angel as 9:1 who opened the shaft) seizes dragon/ancient serpent/devil/Satan, binds, throws into abyss, locks and seals so he “might no longer deceive the nations” until the thousand years complete; then “must” (δεῖ) be released a short time. Thousand years likely **symbolic** of indefinite perfect period (with other Revelation numbers), not woodenly literal (Walvoord/Thomas), though still a real future period for Osborne.  
- *Locus:* 20:1–3 (slice ll. 911–16).  
- *Quote:* “it is likely that this refers to an indefinite but perfect period of time… Satan is completely bound in the abyss and cannot escape.”

**C32.** Against amillennial “partial curtailment during church age” reading of the binding (Mark 3:27; church-age restriction): Osborne argues NT presents Satan as active deceiver/god of this world over unbelievers; 20:3’s cessation of deceiving the nations “does not fit the current situation. Rather, it demands a later period after the parousia.” Nations still exist after 19:21 because **armies**, not all peoples, were slaughtered.  
- *Locus:* 20:1–3 (slice ll. 917–18).  
- *Quote:* “Satan in this age is primarily characterized as the ‘deceiver,’ so 20:3b does not fit the current situation.”

**C33.** **Theodicy of the release:** for a thousand years beast-worshipers live under Christ’s rule without satanic deception; when released they immediately rebel—proving total depravity and necessity of eternal punishment; “the millennium is the judicial evidence that will convict the earth-dwellers.”  
- *Locus:* 20:3; 20:7–8 (slice ll. 918–19, 950).  
- *Quote:* “The purpose is to prove the power of total depravity and demonstrate once and for all the necessity of eternal punishment.”

**C34.** Thrones / first resurrection (20:4–6): those on thrones primarily martyrs as representative of the whole faithful church (all ages), judging/ruling nations; “came to life” = **bodily** resurrection (not conversion or intermediate state—contra Augustine/Hendriksen/Beale’s spiritual reading, which Osborne finds possible but not probable). “First resurrection” = raising of all saints; “rest of the dead” (parenthesis) = unbelievers, conscious next at GWT. Beatitude: second death has no power; priests of God and Christ; reign a thousand years.  
- *Locus:* 20:4–6; n. on 20:4–5 (slice ll. 920–46, 995–97).  
- *Quote:* “Thus, it most likely refers to the resurrection of believers… it is still more viable to see the ‘coming to life’ in 20:4–5 as physical resurrections at the parousia (believers) and last judgment (unbelievers).”

**C35.** Gog and Magog (20:7–10): after millennium Satan released, deceives nations “Gog and Magog” (Ezek. 38–39 fulfillment/transformation—universal, satanic, messianic victory). Gathers for battle “like sand of the sea”; surrounds camp of saints / beloved city (Jerusalem as millennial capital; camp ~ wilderness Israel). **Not** recapitulation of Armageddon (contra Morris/Hendriksen/Beale on same-battle reading of τὸν πόλεμον): second battle—led by Satan not beast; destroyed by fire from heaven not sword from mouth; then devil to lake of fire.  
- *Locus:* 20:7–10 (slice ll. 948–77).  
- *Quote:* “the details are sufficiently different to warrant the view of a second battle rather than a recapitulation of the first.”

**C36.** Devil thrown into lake of fire and sulfur with beast and false prophet; “tormented day and night forever and ever” (collage of 14:10–11)—eternal conscious punishment; “another passage that makes it difficult to accept… annihilation.” False trinity reunited in judgment.  
- *Locus:* 20:10 (slice ll. 972–77).  
- *Quote:* “The picture here is too detailed to mean anything other than eternal punishment… in a billion years, a trillion years, they would do the same!”

**C37.** Great white throne (20:11–15): end of history; throne “great” and “white” (purity/holiness/triumph—last “white” in book); seated one likely God with Christ also involved (throne of God and Lamb). Earth and sky flee; no place found—old order destroyed so new can come (21:1).  
- *Locus:* 20:11 (slice ll. 1036–39).  
- *Quote:* “Before the new age can begin, this age must cease… the new heaven and new earth were able to descend ‘because the first heaven and the first earth have passed away.’”

**C38.** Judgment of the righteous (20:12, on Osborne’s reading): dead great and small before throne; “books” of deeds opened (Dan. 7:10); judged by works—saved by grace, judged by works (Matt. 16:27; Rom. 14:12; 1 Cor. 3; 2 Cor. 5:10; etc.); “book of life” opened (Dan. 12:1–2)—citizenship of heaven. Osborne splits 20:12 (righteous) from 20:13–15 (unrighteous), interlocking with 14:14–20 dual harvest.  
- *Locus:* 20:12 (slice ll. 1041–48).  
- *Quote:* “For believers the theme is simple: we are saved by grace but will be judged by works.”

**C39.** Judgment of sinners (20:13–15): sea, Death, and Hades give up dead; each judged by deeds. Death and Hades thrown into lake of fire = destruction of last enemy (1 Cor. 15:26) and/or malignant personified forces; lake of fire = “second death” (not cessation but ongoing conscious punishment). Anyone not in book of life → lake of fire. Predestination and free will both affirmed: sovereign election **and** conscious rejection of repentance; book belongs to “Lamb slain from the foundation of the world” (13:8).  
- *Locus:* 20:13–15 (slice ll. 1049–58).  
- *Quote:* “The two—the will of humans and the elect will of God—function together here… the unsaved, on the basis of their choices and the judgment of a sovereign God, head into eternal torment.”

**C40.** Theodicy climax of the whole unit: primary thrust of 18:1–19:5 is divine justice and vindication of saints; hallelujahs celebrate true/just judgments; millennial release proves eternal sin demands eternal torment; GWT erases sin so new creation can begin. “Those who are offended by such teaching have too low a realization of the terrible nature of sin and the natural response that divine holiness must have toward it.”  
- *Locus:* 18 summary; 20 summaries; 19 summary (slice ll. 528–29, 848, 979–87, 1060–61).  
- *Quote:* “God’s justice demands this response… God cannot abide sin, and his reaction must be swift and final.”
